query: Which material can be used for enhance glass-forming ability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small amount of interstitial oxygen into a Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti high‐entropy alloy will enhance its glass‐forming ability by promoting local structural disorder and retarding crystallization during rapid solidification.
generation.material_initial_state: Liquid Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi alloy prepared by arc-melting prior to rapid quenching
generation.intervention: Interstitial oxygen doping at controlled sub-stoichiometric levels
generation.conditions: Rapid solidification conditions such as melt spinning under an inert atmosphere with controlled oxygen additions
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of ordered oxygen complexes (interstitial complexes) that induce significant local lattice distortions
generation.mechanism: The interstitial oxygen atoms are expected to create local lattice distortions that impede the nucleation and growth of crystalline phases by stabilizing disordered atomic configurations, thereby widening the critical cooling rate window for glass formation.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in the glass-forming ability of the alloy, observed as a larger supercooled liquid region and/or a reduced tendency for crystallization upon cooling relative to the undoped base alloy.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only at oxygen concentrations low enough to avoid the formation of bulk oxide phases or other deleterious crystallization effects.
generation.uncertainty: While oxygen-induced ordering of interstitial atoms has been shown to modify mechanical damping and strength in related HEAs (as seen in PMC7299626), its direct impact on enhancing the glass-forming ability remains uncertain due to the absence of direct evidence in the provided records.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi alloys with incrementally increased oxygen contents (while maintaining other processing conditions identical), then subject each alloy to rapid quenching (e.g., using melt spinning). Characterize the resulting microstructures by X-ray diffraction, differential scanning calorimetry (to measure the supercooled liquid region), and transmission electron microscopy to detect any crystalline phases.
measurements: Critical cooling rate for amorphous phase formation
Phase identification via XRD and TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If oxygen doping does not lead to a measurable increase in the supercooled liquid region or requires a similar (or higher) critical cooling rate for glass formation compared to the undoped alloy, then the hypothesis that interstitial oxygen enhances the glass‐forming ability would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy alloys be designed to simultaneously achieve high Snoek-type damping capacity, high mechanical strength, and high ductility at elevated temperatures?. System: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi base HEA, (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98O2 (O-2 HEA), and (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98N2 (N-2 HEA). Processing: Arc-melting of pure metals (purity >99.9 wt%), TiN (99.9 wt%), and TiO2 (99.9 wt%) in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere; remelted at least eight times; drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold (10 mm × 10 mm × 60 mm). Test conditions: Damping measured via multifunction internal friction apparatus at 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0 Hz, temperature range 300–1100 K, heating rate 2 K min⁻¹, max strain amplitude 2 × 10⁻⁴; Tensile tests at room temperature, strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Findings: The O-2 HEA achieved a peak damping capacity (tanδ_max) of 0.020 at 1.0 Hz, while the N-2 HEA reached 0.027 at 1.0 Hz.; The N-2 HEA exhibited a yield strength of 1362 MPa and elongation of ~11.9%, while the O-2 HEA showed 1138 MPa yield strength and ~20% elongation.; The peak damping temperature (T_p) for the HEAs was approximately 730–747 K at 1.0 Hz, roughly 100 K higher than traditional Snoe
